question: Which statement best describes Media queries?
options: Media queries apply CSS conditionally based on features of the device, most commonly viewport width. @media (min-width: 768px) { ... } applies its rules only when the viewport is at least 768px wide. They can also test max-width, orientation, prefers-color-scheme, prefers-reduced-motion, and more. They're the core mechanism for adapting layout across breakpoints.

Mobile-first means writing the base styles for small screens first, then layering enhancements with min-width media queries as the screen grows. This keeps the default lightweight, progressively adds complexity, and tends to produce simpler, more maintainable CSS than starting desktop-first with max-width overrides.

Fluid layouts use flexible sizing (%, fr, flex, auto-fit/minmax) so the layout stretches and reflows smoothly between breakpoints instead of jumping. Combining fluid base layout with a few breakpoints gives smooth scaling with targeted structural changes — the modern responsive approach.

Breakpoints are the viewport widths where the layout changes. Rather than targeting specific devices, choose breakpoints where YOUR content starts to look broken (content-driven). Common ranges are roughly ~640px (small), ~768px (tablet), ~1024px (laptop), ~1280px (desktop), but the right values depend on the design.

Without <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> in the HTML head, mobile browsers render the page at a fake ~980px width and shrink it, making media queries effectively useless. This tag tells the browser to use the device's real width as the viewport — it's a prerequisite for any responsive design to work on phones.

question: Which statement best describes Responsive units?
options: min-width queries activate at and above a width (used for mobile-first, adding styles as the screen grows); max-width queries activate at and below a width (desktop-first, overriding down to small screens). Mixing the two carelessly causes overlap conflicts, so most teams pick one direction — usually mobile-first min-width — and stay consistent.

Responsive images serve the right resolution per device to save bandwidth and stay sharp. The img srcset and sizes attributes let the browser pick an appropriately sized file, while <picture> with <source media="..."> enables art direction (different crops per screen). At minimum, make images fluid with max-width: 100%; height: auto so they never overflow.
